claims.statement: John F. Kennedy was born on May 29, 1917, in Brookline, Massachusetts.

A few months before his third birthday he had a serious case of scarlet fever and spent a month in the hospital; through childhood and adolescence he had nausea, joint pain, headaches and diarrhea and was hospitalized several times.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Background only; not used as a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: By 1934 he was sent to the Mayo Clinic, where his bowel illness was diagnosed as colitis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Background for the bowel symptoms and the steroid treatment that followed.

claims.statement: During his college years at Harvard his abdominal pain, weight loss and weakness continued despite a bland diet and strong medicines, including steroids placed under the skin to dissolve.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern history of corticosteroid exposure in his teens and twenties, one reason for the bone density scan.

claims.statement: The historian Robert Dallek, who examined his medical records at the Kennedy Library, believed that many of his difficulties could be traced to corticosteroids taken perhaps as early as 1937 to relieve his colitis, noting that heavy long-term use can promote osteoporosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; supports the modern bone health plan without diagnosing a bone disease.

claims.statement: His chronic back pain began at Harvard, after he was tackled from the side in a football game, possibly damaging a spinal disc; he began wearing a corset brace to stabilize his spine.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern chronic low back pain and the brace.

claims.statement: His back and intestinal problems caused him to fail Army and Navy physical examinations, but he was admitted to the Navy in October 1941. In August 1943 the patrol torpedo boat he commanded, PT-109, was struck by a Japanese destroyer; he led the survivors to safety, and his back worsened as a result.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the worsening of the back pain.

claims.statement: He came home from the war in the Pacific thin and sallow from malaria.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past history; the malaria was later given as the public explanation for the 1947 illness.

claims.statement: Against the advice of his doctors at the Mayo Clinic, he had spinal surgery in June 1944 at New England Baptist Hospital; about six weeks later the pain returned.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern history of persistent low back pain after lumbar disc surgery.

claims.statement: In 1946, at 29, he was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives from a Boston district. During the campaign his back was so bad that he wore a brace and used daily hot baths and massage.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern work history and the brace.

claims.statement: In 1947, at 30, while a congressman, he collapsed on a visit to England; a doctor there diagnosed Addison's disease and told one of his friends that he might not live a year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic modern diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency during a crisis abroad.

source_links.locator: In 1947 J.F.K., then 30, learned he had Addison's disease

claims.statement: Returning to America aboard the Queen Mary, he was so ill that a priest was called to give him the last rites.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Shows how serious the first crisis was; the modern episode records a crisis treated in hospital.

source_links.locator: a priest had also been called in 1947

claims.statement: He passed off the illness as a recurrence of his wartime malaria. In Boston an endocrinologist began treating him for Addison's disease with pellets of a synthetic adrenal hormone, desoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA), implanted under his skin.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern start of replacement treatment soon after the diagnosis and his wish to decide who knows.

claims.statement: By 1950, when cortisone was available by mouth, he also took 25 mg of cortisone each day.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: In October 1954 he had a spinal fusion with a metal plate; he developed a urinary tract infection and became so ill that a priest was called to give him the last rites, and he later developed a staphylococcal wound infection. In February 1955 the plate was removed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: He was diagnosed with hypothyroidism during a hospital stay in New York in 1955, and he is reported to have taken liothyronine throughout his presidency.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date. Why the modern record screens for autoimmune thyroid disease and finds it.

claims.statement: Dr. Janet Travell, who first saw him in May 1955 and later became his White House physician, treated his back with injections of procaine into the muscles; Pait and Dowdy write that he received hundreds, if not thousands, of injections over about four years, which with muscle strengthening and the corset brought marked improvement.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history. Medicines are recorded only as the sources state them.

claims.statement: Through his years in Congress and the Senate he denied rumors that he had Addison's disease. During the 1960 campaign his campaign issued a statement that denied he had Addison's disease, describing it as a tuberculous destruction of the adrenal gland, and called his health excellent; in 1960 he acknowledged an adrenal deficiency.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history. The modern episode respects his choice about who is told.

claims.statement: Dallek reported that during his presidency he took many medicines each day: steroids for his Addison's disease, painkillers for his back, antispasmodics for his colitis, antibiotics for urinary tract infections, and antihistamines for allergies.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history, in Dallek's words as Time quotes them. No other drug is named in this record.

claims.statement: From late 1961 Dr. Hans Kraus put him on a program of exercise, swimming, massage and heat and tried to wean him off the back brace, with marked improvement; in August 1963 he strained his back and wore the brace again.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history. The modern back pain plan follows current guidance, not his treatment.

claims.statement: He was assassinated in Dallas on November 22, 1963.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; not used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Reviewing his medical records in 2009, Lee Mandel concluded that his Addison's disease and his hypothyroidism were most likely parts of a single autoimmune disorder, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation, linked to his later hypothyroidism; the modern episode screens for associated autoimmune disease because the guideline advises it for anyone with this diagnosis.

claims.statement: Macchia and colleagues proposed that his bowel symptoms from adolescence fit well with coeliac disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and unproven; one reason the modern episode includes celiac serology, which is negative.

claims.statement: Retrospective reviews of his back disagree. The physician who reviewed the records with Dallek said he had compression fractures in his low back and osteoporosis; Pait and Dowdy, reviewing his X-rays, found no sign of underlying bone disease or of a steroid-related fracture and judged that his four back operations (a discectomy, a fusion with instrumentation, and two smaller operations) failed to relieve his pain.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and disputed; the modern bone density scan is within the expected range, and no bone disease is diagnosed.

claims.statement: Pinals and Hassett argued in 2013 that, because operations on the presumed structural cause brought little relief and a conservative program with trigger point injections and exercise helped modestly, his pain is better understood through current pain research than as a purely structural problem.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; consistent with the modern exercise-based back pain plan.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Kennedy returns two weeks after his first visit and is seen by Dr. Desai of endocrinology on the same day. He takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg at 2 pm and fludrocortisone half a tablet each morning, as the hospital prescribed, and has missed no doses. His energy is better than at discharge but fades by late afternoon. He craves salty food and feels lightheaded for a few seconds when he stands up quickly; he has not fainted. His appetite is good and he has gained a little weight. He has no nausea or abdominal pain. He started physical therapy last week and has done his exercises daily; his back still aches after long sitting and he wears the brace for the drive to work. He uses acetaminophen once or twice a day. He has practised with the trainer injection kit. He had his bone density scan this morning.

referral.question: Primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed about three months ago during an adrenal crisis abroad, in a 30-year-old legislator still on his hospital doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, with signs of mineralocorticoid under-replacement and a raised TSH. Please confirm the cause, set the replacement doses, advise on the thyroid result and bone health, and plan stress dosing and follow-up
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: While traveling abroad about three months ago he collapsed with vomiting, low blood pressure and confusion and was admitted with an adrenal crisis; the discharge letter reports a low morning cortisol with a markedly raised ACTH, low sodium and high potassium before the first dose, and no cosyntropin test. He was discharged on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg at 2 pm and fludrocortisone 0.05 mg daily. Since then he has gained some strength but tires by late afternoon and craves salt. Background: colitis in his teens treated with corticosteroids, including steroid pellets under the skin in college; chronic low back pain since a football injury in college, worse after wartime naval service, with a lumbar operation that did not relieve it; malaria in the Pacific. Today: weight 66.0 kg, blood pressure 104/66 seated with a postural fall, darkened palmar creases and gums. Results today: sodium 134, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, eGFR 109, fasting glucose 84 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL; plasma renin activity 9.6 ng/mL/h; 21-hydroxylase antibodies 18 U/mL (positive); TSH 7.4 mIU/L, free T4 1.0 ng/dL, thyroid peroxidase antibodies 286 IU/mL; vitamin B12 455 pg/mL; A1c 5.1%; tissue transglutaminase IgA 1.1 U/mL with total IgA 214 mg/dL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 31 ng/mL. Oswestry 32%, PHQ-9 4. A bone density scan is booked for the morning of your visit. He was given an emergency hydrocortisone kit and written sick-day rules today. He wants to decide himself who is told about his diagnosis
questions: Do the pre-treatment results and the positive 21-hydroxylase antibodies settle the diagnosis and its cause, or is further testing needed?
What hydrocortisone dose and timing do you advise, given he is on 30 mg a day from the hospital?
Should fludrocortisone be increased, given the raised renin, low sodium, high potassium and postural drop?
How should the raised TSH with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies be handled, and when is it safe to start thyroid hormone?
Does he need bone protection after earlier corticosteroid exposure, and how should bone health be followed?
What sick-day, surgical stress-dose and follow-up plan, including screening for other autoimmune disease, do you advise?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Kennedy, a 30-year-old legislator, is seen at the request of Dr. Prescott about three months after an adrenal crisis abroad. He takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg at 2 pm and fludrocortisone 0.05 mg daily without missed doses. His energy is better but fades by late afternoon; he craves salt and feels lightheaded for a few seconds on standing quickly. He has had no nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain since discharge. He had corticosteroids for colitis in his teens and twenties. He has no symptoms of diabetes, anemia, or celiac disease. He has practised with the trainer injection kit. He wants to keep working full days and to keep the diagnosis private except from people he chooses
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Prescott's intake note and the hospital discharge letter (low morning cortisol with markedly raised ACTH before treatment, low sodium, high potassium). assessment.assessment: The low cortisol with a markedly raised ACTH before treatment, with low sodium and high potassium, establishes primary adrenal insufficiency, and the positive 21-hydroxylase antibodies establish an autoimmune cause. A cosyntropin test would need treatment to be stopped and adds nothing; adrenal imaging and other causes need not be pursued with positive antibodies. Glucocorticoid replacement is more than he needs at 30 mg a day; mineralocorticoid replacement is too low, shown by salt craving, the postural drop, the electrolytes and the raised renin

assessment.display: Raised TSH with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies
assessment.assessment: Probable autoimmune thyroiditis, which often accompanies autoimmune adrenal insufficiency. A raised TSH can settle once glucocorticoid replacement is established, but he has been on replacement for three months, so this is likely to be true thyroid disease. A newly raised TSH should be confirmed before treatment; levothyroxine is safe to start because glucocorticoid replacement is in place, and it must never be started before it

assessment.display: Chronic low back pain; bone health
assessment.assessment: His Z-scores are within the expected range for his age, so there is no sign of bone loss from his earlier corticosteroids. Physiological replacement at 15 to 25 mg of hydrocortisone a day does not need bone-protective medicine; over-replacement is what should be avoided

recommendations: No further diagnostic testing for the adrenal insufficiency: the cause is autoimmune
Reduce hydrocortisone to 10 mg on waking, 5 mg at noon and 5 mg at 4 pm (20 mg a day), adjusted by weight, energy and signs of over- or under-replacement rather than by cortisol levels
Increase fludrocortisone to 0.1 mg once daily; check sodium, potassium, renin and lying and standing blood pressure in about six weeks, aiming for renin in the upper normal range
Repeat TSH and free T4 at the six-week visit; if the TSH is still raised, start levothyroxine 50 mcg daily and check TSH six weeks later
No bone-protective medicine; calcium and vitamin D from diet, weight-bearing exercise, and no repeat scan unless his dose rises or he has a fracture

Sick-day rules: double the hydrocortisone for fever above 38 °C and triple it above 39 °C until a day after the fever settles; inject 100 mg into the thigh and call 911 for vomiting, inability to take tablets, or feeling faint. For surgery or dental work under general anesthesia, or a major illness in hospital, hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously at induction and then 200 mg a day by infusion or divided doses until he is eating, tapering back over one to two days
Carry the injection kit, a steroid emergency card and a medical ID at all times, with spare tablets when traveling
Screen for associated autoimmune disease: TSH at least yearly, and vitamin B12, A1c and celiac serology yearly or with symptoms
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Prescott, who sees him the same day. The plan and the sick-day rules were explained to Mr. Kennedy, who agreed and demonstrated a practice injection; he decides who else receives this note
consultant_note.follow_up: Endocrinology review in one year, or sooner for an adrenal crisis or a change in the thyroid results; Dr. Prescott continues prescribing and monitoring and will share the six-week results
